comments.author: Dicethrower
comments.body:
To bring it back to gamedev. Whenever you're making something, you have about 5 phases.

* Brainstorming to an idea.
* Design on paper.
* Labor to make the thing.
* Testing.
* Polishing for final "game feel".

AI is only decent at replacing the labor part. Maybe with Fable some of the design on paper can now also be done, but only if it's a relatively common feature and you heavily supervise. Either way, it's terrible at brainstorming, and it obviously cannot test or polish a game designed for humans.

People complain about the quality of AI because they're seeing the results of developers using AI for the wrong steps, or completely ignoring the follow up steps they still need to do. This is no different than if they don't do those steps properly while doing everything manually. You're going to get shit.

Ultimately, what we're doing is putting ideas into something real that you can put in people's hands. Creators just wants to turn their ideas into something real, and shouldn't really care about what tools they use to do it. Likewise (most) consumers don't care about anything other than the end result.

So long as AI can't come up with ideas, and the end result still clearly depends on the skill level of the tool user,  arguing over whether some tool does too much, and whether you can still call yourself a programmer/designer/creator/etc, is arguing from tradition. This is itself always pointless, because it'll always depend on whatever you personally feel like something should be.
